claims.claim: Composition is the arrangement of visual elements on the picture plane so that the parts read as one unified whole; the picture plane is the flat surface (paper, canvas, screen) on which the image is created, and figure-ground describes the separation of a positive subject from the negative space around it.

A focal point is the element that catches the viewer's attention first, produced by contrast in size, color, value, texture, or isolation; movement is the path the viewer's eye takes through the work, often toward focal areas, directed by lines, edges, shapes, and colors.

Negative space (the ground) is an active compositional element, not leftover emptiness; positive shapes are read as the figure and negative shapes as the space around them, a distinction rooted in Gestalt figure-ground perception.

The term 'rule of thirds' was coined by the painter and engraver John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery, extending an observation by Sir Joshua Reynolds about the ratio of light to dark; Smith proposed a roughly two-thirds to one-third proportion and hedged the term ('if I may be allowed so to call it'). It is a convention, not a proven law.

Empirical support for a human aesthetic preference for golden-section proportions is weak and highly sensitive to careless experimental method; Gustav Fechner's 1876 rectangle-preference results did not hold up reliably in later, better-controlled studies.

Many popular claims that the golden ratio pervades great art, architecture (the Parthenon, the Great Pyramid), and nature are retrofitted, exaggerated, or poorly referenced and passed uncritically between authors; the golden ratio is best treated as a heuristic, not an evidence-based key to beauty.

The format (proportion and shape of the frame) is itself a compositional decision; changing format, for example from landscape to portrait, can require a different arrangement of the same elements, and the edges crop and shape the whole composition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the golden ratio has any genuine aesthetic effect on human preference.
positions: Popular design literature asserts a strong, near-universal preference and pervasive appearance in art and nature.
Green's review of over a century of experiments concludes any effect is weak and methodologically fragile, and many historical 'appearances' are retrofitted.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows Green: it presents the golden ratio and dynamic symmetry as heuristics whose importance is overstated, attributes the skepticism, and does not assert the ubiquity claims.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('a foundational concept', 'a simple way to apply it') with no substantive, verifiable claims about composition; essentially all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced boilerplate definitions with a substantive account of the frame, picture plane, figure-ground, focal points, cropping, and unity.
Added the documented 1797 origin of the rule of thirds rather than presenting it as a bare rule.
Added attributed skepticism about the golden ratio and dynamic symmetry instead of treating design conventions as laws.
Handed off balance, visual hierarchy, and grid/layout to their own topics to avoid duplication.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding Formal Analysis: Principles of Design
sourceRecords.provider: The J. Paul Getty Museum (Education at the Getty)
sourceRecords.notes: Museum education resource read via WebFetch (HTML page). Supports the definitions used for balance ('the distribution of the visual weight of objects, colors, textures, and space'), emphasis/focal point ('the part of the design that catches the viewer's attention'), and movement ('the path the viewer's eye takes through the work of art, often to focal areas'). Companion PDF (building_lessons/principles_design.pdf) covers the same principles. Copyrighted; used only for definitions, no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Reading: Artistic Elements (Art Appreciation)
sourceRecords.notes: Open educational resource ('Artistic Elements' authored by Christopher Gildow, CC BY-NC-SA) read via WebFetch. Supports the definitions of the picture plane ('the flat surface an image is created upon; a piece of paper, stretched canvas, wood panel'), the figure-ground relationship, and positive/negative space (hand example: the hand is the positive shape, the surrounding space the negative shape). Used reference-only for facts; no prose reproduced given the NC-SA terms.

sourceRecords.title: All That Glitters: A Review of Psychological Research on the Aesthetics of the Golden Section
sourceRecords.provider: Christopher D. Green, Perception, vol. 24, no. 8, pp. 937-968
sourceRecords.notes: Peer-reviewed review article (Perception, 1995). Author's copy at https://www.yorku.ca/christo/papers/Green.golden.Perception-1995.pdf. Supports the conclusion that any real aesthetic effect of the golden section is weak and 'relatively sensitive to careless methodological practices', and that Fechner's 1876 rectangle-preference findings did not replicate reliably under better controls. Verified via the SAGE abstract, the York University author pages, and web search of the article; PDF text extraction was not available in this environment, so the abstract and companion pages were used. Copyrighted; facts synthesized in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Background to 'All That Glitters': Historical Claims About the Golden Section
sourceRecords.notes: Companion background page by the paper's author, read via WebFetch. Supports the point that many golden-section claims are poorly referenced and passed uncritically between authors (e.g., Ghyka), that Egyptian/Great-Pyramid theoretical knowledge of phi is doubtful, and that botanical (phyllotaxis) claims were challenged (Mitchison vs. D'Arcy Thompson). Used to frame the ubiquity claims as largely myth.

sourceRecords.title: Rule of thirds (encyclopedia article with primary-source quotations)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the Wikipedia raw wikitext (index.php?action=raw). Used only for the well-documented historical fact that the term 'rule of thirds' was coined by John Thomas Smith in his 1797 book Remarks on Rural Scenery, extending Reynolds's observation on light/dark ratio, and that Smith hedged the term. The article reproduces the primary sources (Smith 1797, Reynolds 1783, Field's 1845 Chromatics), which are public-domain historical texts. Corroborated by B&H Explora and Fstoppers histories. Only the historical fact is used.
